abstract: Choosing a DNN accelerator dataflow requires reasoning about scheduling, placement, reuse, and the hardware that can support them. A stationary-data label cannot capture how layer dimensions interact with buffering, communication bandwidth, and parallelism. MAESTRO makes these relationships explicit through TemporalMap, SpatialMap, and Cluster directives. From workload, mapping, and hardware inputs, its analytical model derives reuse and communication opportunities at each hierarchy level and estimates runtime, activity counts, energy, buffer requirements, and utilization. Opportunities become useful only when multicast, reductions, buffers, and bandwidth provide the required support. Runtime validation against a 64-PE MAERI RTL simulation on VGG16 and reported Eyeriss runtimes on AlexNet yields average absolute error within 3.9% for those comparisons. A modeled study of five dataflow styles across operators from five DNN models finds potential runtime and energy reductions of 37% and 10% through adaptive choices. Hardware exploration varies PE count, buffers, and NoC bandwidth under area and power constraints, skipping infeasible regions through cost lower bounds. One KC-P/VGG16-CONV2 search reports 3,936,256 explored points, 175,861 valid points, and 12.20 minutes; explored points are not full simulations. MAESTRO thus supports analytical comparison of mappings and hardware configurations. The validation does not establish universal prediction accuracy or measured energy accuracy, and automatic dataflow tuning and RTL generation remain future work.
introduction: A DNN accelerator's dataflow specifies when tensor computations execute and where they are placed. That decision determines opportunities for spatial reuse and temporal reuse, but their value depends on the operator dimensions and the supporting machine. A mapping that exposes multicast or reduction opportunities cannot realize them without suitable communication hardware, just as reuse cannot compensate for an unsuitable buffer capacity. More PEs or more buffering alone may therefore leave a bandwidth-constrained design unimproved. These interactions make stationary-data labels insufficient for comparing complete mappings. In the broader setting of systematic accelerator evaluation [parashar2019timeloop], the challenge addressed here is to express a mapping precisely enough to connect its reuse opportunities to runtime and resource requirements.

MAESTRO represents dataflow with TemporalMap, SpatialMap, and Cluster directives. Given a workload, mapping, and hardware configuration, the analysis derives tensor reuse and communication opportunities at each hierarchy level. It then estimates runtime, activity counts, energy, buffer requirements, and utilization, connecting placement and scheduling choices to the resources that sustain them. Energy estimates combine activity counts with component energy estimates; design-space experiments also use synthesized component area and power costs. The same framework explores PE count, local and shared buffer capacity, and NoC bandwidth under area and power constraints. Cost lower bounds allow the search to skip infeasible regions. This enables comparison of interdependent hardware choices without equating every explored point with a full simulation, or treating abstract dataflow comparisons as measurements of manufactured accelerators.

We validate runtime predictions against a 64-PE MAERI RTL simulation on VGG16 and reported Eyeriss runtimes on AlexNet. Average absolute runtime error is within 3.9% for these comparisons, which neither establishes a bound across all dataflows nor validates energy error. A modeled comparison of five dataflow styles on operators from five DNN models shows that preferred mappings change with operator characteristics; adaptive choices offer potential runtime and energy reductions of 37% and 10% in that case study. Hardware search experiments use an Intel i7-8700K with 32 GB memory, synthesized 28 nm component costs, and constraints of 16 mm² and 450 mW. In the KC-P/VGG16-CONV2 run, the search explores 3,936,256 points, identifies 175,861 valid points, and takes 12.20 minutes. Those constraints describe the searched hardware, not overhead imposed by MAESTRO. The demonstrated contribution is an analytical exploration tool; automatic dataflow tuning and RTL generation remain future capabilities.
